opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it started out as pure curiosity. When I watched Karpathy's "Zero to Hero" videos, the thing that struck me was how he demystified everything. He'd write a bigram model in a notebook, then build up to attention, then to a small GPT, and at every step you could see exactly what was happening. I came away thinking, "This isn't magic. It's code I can actually write."

So my first approach was just to follow along line by line. No copy-pasting. I typed everything out myself, broke it, fixed it, and made sure I understood why each piece was there. I think that's underrated. You learn far more from debugging your own shape mismatch at two in the morning than from reading a clean implementation.

After that, the ambition grew a bit. I asked myself, what would it take to train something that's actually useful, not just a toy that generates Shakespeare-ish text? That's when you run into the real problems: data, compute, and engineering. With data, you realize quickly that quality matters much more than you'd expect. Cleaning, deduplicating, and filtering took up a huge share of my time. Compute was the hard constraint. As an individual, you don't have a cluster, so you have to be very deliberate. I spent a lot of time on small-scale experiments, trying to understand scaling behavior before spending money on anything bigger. And with engineering, things like mixed precision, gradient accumulation, checkpointing, and making sure a run doesn't silently diverge suddenly matter a lot. None of it is glamorous, but it's where most of the actual work is.

The mindset shift for me was going from "I want to train a big model" to "I want to deeply understand every decision in the training pipeline." Once I framed it that way, the size of the model mattered less. Even a small model trained carefully teaches you a lot about how the big labs think.

I'd also say community helped enormously. People share training logs, ablations, and failure stories openly, and reading those saved me from making many mistakes myself. So it was a mix of hands-on building, being honest about my constraints, and learning from people who'd already gone a few steps further down the road.

r001.rationale: The response describes wanting to train a useful model and deeply understand the training pipeline, but does not state an ambition to train the best model among similarly tiny models.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the ambition came before the ability. I watched Karpathy's "Zero to Hero" series — the micrograd one, then makemore, then the GPT-from-scratch video — and by the end of it I had this feeling that I understood everything. Which was completely false. I understood it the way you understand a magic trick after someone explains it: you nod, and then you try to do it yourself and your hands don't work.

So the first thing I did was the dumbest possible thing, which was to re-type his code. Not copy-paste, actually type it, line by line, pausing the video. That sounds trivial, but it forced me to notice every place where I would have done something different and been wrong. Why is the mask a lower-triangular matrix. Why do you divide by the square root of the head dimension. Why does the loss start at roughly ln of the vocabulary size. Those little "huh" moments were the real curriculum.

After that I set a rule for myself: I wasn't allowed to train anything on a dataset I didn't care about. Shakespeare is fine for a tutorial, but I had no emotional stake in whether the model produced good fake Shakespeare. So I scraped a few years of my own chat logs and notes — in Chinese, which immediately broke everything, because character-level tokenization on Chinese behaves totally differently than on English. That was my first real lesson: the tutorial gives you a model, but the data gives you the problems, and the problems are where you actually learn.

Then I hit the wall everyone hits, which is compute. I had one consumer GPU. I spent probably two weeks just convincing myself that a tiny model trained properly was more interesting than a bigger model trained badly. Karpathy says this almost offhand, but it took me a long time to believe it. So I trained something around ten million parameters, watched the loss curve obsessively, and learned to read it like a doctor reads a heartbeat — when the learning rate is too high, when you're overfitting, when the data has duplicates in it.

The honest answer to "how did I approach it" is: I lowered my ambition until it fit inside what I could actually run, and then I slowly raised it back up. The thing that changed wasn't the goal. It was that I stopped treating "train a language model" as one big step and started treating it as about two hundred small, boring, verifiable ones.

r001.rationale: The response says he trained a roughly ten-million-parameter model, but does not state that his ambition was to make it the best language model among models of similarly tiny size.

astra-6.text: I approached it as a learning project first. Watching Karpathy’s series made me want to build something myself, but there’s a big gap between following an explanation and getting a model to train. So I tried to make the ambition smaller and more concrete: start with a simple model, understand the training process, and work up from there. The first goal was to get something working that I could actually understand.
